title: Storage Systems: Allocation, Lifecycle, Retention, and Backup
bodyMarkdown:
## Storage is a decision about access pattern, cost and recoverability

The exam tests four skills here: matching a workload to a storage product, driving cost down with classes and lifecycle rules, proving compliance with retention controls, and moving or protecting data within a deadline and an RPO/RTO. Most wrong answers are plausible tools applied to the wrong constraint, for example Object Versioning offered as WORM, or a network transfer offered for a volume the link can never carry.

## Matching storage to the workload

| Need | Product | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Unstructured objects, backups, data lakes, static assets | Cloud Storage | Object store; classes and lifecycle control cost |
| VM boot and data disks | Persistent Disk or [Hyperdisk](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/disks/hyperdisks) | Block storage; Hyperdisk lets you pick IOPS and throughput per volume |
| Shared POSIX file system over NFS | [Filestore](https://cloud.google.com/filestore/docs/service-tiers) | NFSv3 and NFSv4.1; zonal and regional tiers; backups and snapshots supported |
| Relational and NoSQL databases | Cloud SQL, AlloyDB, Spanner, Bigtable, Firestore | Chosen in domain 1; here you provision, back up and protect them |

**Hyperdisk** comes in Balanced (the recommended default for most enterprise applications), Balanced High Availability (cross-zonal replication within a region), Extreme (highest IOPS for demanding databases), Throughput (analytics) and ML (read-only multi-attach to many instances). The distinguishing feature versus Persistent Disk is that you set IOPS and throughput **independently** of capacity, can change them while the volume is attached, and get provisioned performance immediately. **Hyperdisk Storage Pools** buy capacity in bulk to avoid overprovisioning. Support is tied to machine series: newer series such as C4, M3 and M4 are supported, while older series such as N1 and E2 have limited support, so check the machine type before promising a disk type.

## Cloud Storage classes

All classes share 99.999999999% annual durability, millisecond access (even Archive, "not hours or days"), and no minimum object size. They differ in price structure, minimum storage duration and retrieval fees. See [storage classes](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/storage-classes).

| Class | Minimum duration | Typical access | Retrieval fee | Use |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Standard | None | Frequent | No | Hot data, websites, active analytics |
| Nearline | 30 days | About once a month or less | Yes | Backups, long-tail content |
| Coldline | 90 days | About once a quarter | Yes | Infrequently read archives |
| Archive | 365 days | Less than once a year | Yes | Compliance and disaster recovery copies |

Deleting or moving an object before its minimum duration triggers an early-deletion charge (soft-deleted Standard objects are exempt). Availability SLAs vary by location type; for example Standard is 99.95% for multi-region and dual-region, 99.9% for a single region. The newer Rapid Storage class exists only for zonal Rapid buckets and targets AI and analytics workloads needing significantly lower latency and higher throughput; it is not a general archival choice.

## Lifecycle management and Autoclass

[Object Lifecycle Management](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/lifecycle) evaluates rules made of conditions and an action:

- **Conditions** include `age`, `createdBefore`, `isLive`, `numNewerVersions`, `matchesStorageClass`, `daysSinceNoncurrentTime`, prefix and suffix matching, size thresholds, and custom-time conditions.
- **Actions** are `Delete`, `SetStorageClass` and `AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload`.
- Class transitions only move **warmer to colder** (Standard to Nearline to Coldline to Archive). `SetStorageClass` is billed as a Class A operation, but time already spent in the original class counts toward the next class's minimum duration, and no retrieval or early-deletion fee is charged.
- Execution is **asynchronous**: there can be a lag between the condition being met and the action running. Lifecycle respects retention policies and holds, delaying actions until they clear.

**Worked example.** Logs are read heavily for 30 days, occasionally for the next 11 months, and kept 7 years: Standard, `age` 30 to Nearline, `age` 365 to Coldline or Archive, `Delete` at roughly 2,555 days. Going Nearline straight to Archive at 365 days is also a valid shape; the pattern (progressively colder with age, then delete), not the exact tiers, is what the exam checks.

[Autoclass](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/autoclass) removes the need to know the pattern. Objects start in Standard, move to Nearline after 30 days without access, and (with Archive as the terminal class) to Coldline at 90 days and Archive at 365 days; reading an object returns it to Standard. Objects under 128 KiB stay in Standard. A management fee applies, but retrieval and early-deletion fees are generally waived and class transitions are free. Constraints: you **cannot** use `SetStorageClass` lifecycle rules on an Autoclass bucket. Autoclass is for unpredictable access; if you already know which data is archival, explicit lifecycle rules are cheaper and more predictable.

## Retention, holds and recovery from mistakes

Distinguish compliance controls from operational safety nets:

- **Retention policy** sets a minimum age before objects can be deleted or replaced. It applies to existing and new objects. The maximum retention period is 3,155,760,000 seconds (100 years).
- **Bucket Lock** (locking the retention policy) is **irreversible**: after locking you can increase the period but never reduce or remove it, even as the project owner. You cannot delete the bucket until every object has met its retention, and a project lien blocks project deletion. This is the WORM answer. See [Bucket Lock](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/bucket-lock).
- **Object Retention Lock** defines retention per object rather than per bucket, and can coexist with a bucket policy. Holds (event-based and temporary) pause deletion on specific objects.
- **[Soft delete](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/soft-delete)** is on by default with a **7-day** retention window (configurable from 7 to 90 days; 0 disables it). It covers deleted objects and buckets, but soft-deleted data keeps accruing storage charges, so disable it for temporary data. It is a safety net, not compliance immutability.
- **Object Versioning** keeps noncurrent versions after overwrite or delete. Combine it with lifecycle rules (`numNewerVersions`, `daysSinceNoncurrentTime`) or storage grows without bound.

## Moving data in

Choose by data size, link speed and deadline:

| Method | Use when |
|---|---|
| `gcloud storage` (parallel composite uploads) | Smaller datasets, ad hoc, link is sufficient |
| [Storage Transfer Service](https://cloud.google.com/storage-transfer/docs/overview) | Online transfers above about 1 TiB from S3, Azure Blob, HTTP lists, other buckets, or on-premises file systems and HDFS via self-hosted agents; scheduled, event-driven, preserves metadata, validates integrity |
| [Transfer Appliance](https://cloud.google.com/transfer-appliance/docs/4.0/overview) | The network would need more than one week, or the link is shared and slow |

Transfer Appliance comes in TA40 and TA300 models. You copy data over NFS (Linux and macOS) or SCP/SSH (Windows), ship it back, and Google uploads it to your bucket and securely erases the device (NIST 800-88). Data is AES-256 encrypted and can use customer-managed keys from Cloud KMS. The documented illustration: 300 TB over 100 Mbps would take around nine months online but under 25 days with the appliance, and data is typically available within about 10 business days of the return shipment. An online mode can stream from the appliance to the bucket without shipping. Do the arithmetic from the stem: a fully saturated 1 Gbps link carries roughly 10 TB per day, so a few hundred TB on a link also needed by production is a Transfer Appliance case, not a Storage Transfer Service case.

## Backup and recovery

- **[Backup and DR Service](https://cloud.google.com/backup-disaster-recovery/docs/concepts/backup-dr)** is the centralized, policy-driven answer. A **backup plan** (rules with hourly through yearly frequency, windows and retention) is attached to workloads and writes to a **backup vault**, a Google-managed isolated store that enforces WORM immutability with a minimum enforced retention of up to 99 years. It protects Compute Engine instances and Persistent Disk, Cloud SQL, AlloyDB, Filestore, VMware Engine VMs, self-managed databases and Bare Metal Solution, provides application-consistent backups, multi-region replication, and CMEK for Compute Engine, Persistent Disk and Cloud SQL. Cloud Storage is not listed as a directly supported backup source.
- **[Disk snapshots](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/disks/snapshots)** are incremental. Standard snapshots are geo-redundant, persist after the source disk is deleted and suit disaster recovery; archive snapshots are cheaper for long-term retention; instant snapshots are zonal or regional, vanish with the source disk, and suit fast recovery from user error. Standard snapshot deletion has a three-day recycle bin (listed as a preview feature); archive snapshot deletion is permanent.
- **[Cloud SQL backups](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/backup-recovery/backups)** are automated or on-demand. Automated retention runs from 1 to 365 days for standard backups (up to 10 years for enhanced backups). Do not delete automated backups manually because point-in-time recovery depends on them. Restoring targets a new or an existing instance, with a matching database version. Retained backups survive instance deletion.

## Anti-patterns and common mistakes

- **Archive from day one for data that is still being read.** Retrieval fees and the 365-day minimum duration make it more expensive than Standard.
- **Versioning or soft delete as WORM.** Neither prevents a privileged user from deleting; only a locked retention policy does.
- **Locking a retention policy before testing it.** A lock is permanent and cannot be shortened; trial with an unlocked policy first.
- **Autoclass plus `SetStorageClass` rules.** Not allowed on the same bucket; pick one mechanism.
- **Pushing hundreds of terabytes through a shared WAN link.** Do the bandwidth math; use Transfer Appliance.
- **Manual snapshot cron with no retention.** It grows unbounded and is not application-consistent or centrally governed; use Backup and DR backup plans.
- **Leaving soft delete on for scratch buckets.** Deleted temporary data still bills for the retention window.
- **Assuming Hyperdisk everywhere.** Older machine series support fewer types.

## Exam tips

- **WORM or "nobody can shorten retention" means retention policy plus lock.** Versioning, soft delete and IAM trust are distractors.
- **Cost-optimized aging data means lifecycle transitions or Autoclass.** Known pattern: explicit lifecycle rules; unknown or varied pattern: Autoclass. Never both on one bucket for class changes.
- **Memorize the minimum durations:** Nearline 30, Coldline 90, Archive 365 days. Early-deletion charges follow from them.
- **Data above a week of network transfer means Transfer Appliance.** Online recurring or large cloud-to-cloud moves use Storage Transfer Service; small ad hoc uploads use `gcloud storage`.
- **Centralized, policy-driven, application-consistent VM backups means Backup and DR Service** with a backup plan and vault; add Cloud SQL automated backups and PITR for databases.
- **Soft delete defaults to 7 days** and is an accident safety net, not a compliance control.
- **Independent IOPS and throughput tuning means Hyperdisk.** Shared NFS means Filestore.
- **Class transitions only go colder.** A lifecycle rule cannot move Archive back to Standard; Autoclass can, on access.
